discovery: Discovery and development of metal-halide perovskite semiconductors for efficient solar energy conversion
subfield: Condensed matter and materials physics (semiconductor optoelectronics)
motivation: In 2009 Miyasaka showed that solution-processed organic-inorganic lead halide perovskites absorb light and generate photovoltage, going against the belief that a soft, defect-rich ionic crystal could not be a good semiconductor. In 2012 Park and Snaith, in independent work with Miyasaka, made solid-state devices and found long carrier diffusion lengths and ambipolar transport, which showed that the perovskite itself is the working semiconductor. Power-conversion efficiency then rose from 3.8% to above 26%, a speed without precedent in photovoltaics, and perovskite-silicon tandems now exceed 33%. The work revealed new physics: defect tolerance, large polarons, weak non-radiative recombination and ion migration in a low-temperature-processed crystal. It opened a field of light emitters, detectors and lasers. Like other good materials discoveries, it came from chemical intuition and gave both new fundamental physics and a technology that is now being commercialised.
